text: After this you can use the same scenario to test several engineering ideas.

A repeated scenario helps compare different engineering tools without changing the underlying problem. Begin with a system boundary and outside links. Then examine cooperating systems, form requirements and map major life-cycle work. Group discussion exposes differences in stakeholder assumptions rather than proving one answer by popularity.

items: Choose one fictional operational problem and define its purpose. You should see: A short statement of intended use. If not: Name the people affected and the operating conditions.
Sketch its components and outside connections. You should see: A boundary with each critical exchange named. If not: Look for an omitted support or information connection.
Write one measurable requirement and its test. You should see: A link from need to evidence. If not: Separate multiple outcomes into separate requirements.
Trace one change into service and retirement. You should see: An identified support consequence. If not: Ask who maintains the changed element.
Inferred: A community transport service relies on vehicles, scheduling, operators and maintenance. Its boundary depends on the decision.

text: Reuse one scenario to expose how engineering views connect.
A workshop sketch is not final design evidence.

items: Treating group agreement as proof. An untested assumption can survive discussion. Fix: Assign a test or information owner.
